findings.where: First screen, top-left lockup (name and logo), desktop and phone
findings.fault: The logo is bigger and heavier than Mark's name, so the logo leads and not his name. The name is set at about the nav's size, and the white arches beside it are the strongest shape in the header. On first sight the eye reads 'MMM Infra' as whose site this is.
findings.who_objects: The founder and Mark: the brief's personal-advisor test asks for his name to lead with the logo beside it, because the individual is the brand (brand sheet §5). A bank official scanning the header takes the firm as the brand.

findings.where: First screen header, the logo on the slate hero
findings.fault: The mark and wordmark have been turned warm-white to sit on the dark ground. The client does not hold a white version of the logo, and nothing records that Mark agreed to one. The footer shows the real colours (grey arches, blue wordmark), so the page uses two versions of his logo.
findings.who_objects: Mark, as the logo's owner: under the house's never-recolour rule, a version the client does not hold is made only with the client's yes. The v7 card does not grant one, unlike v4's.

findings.where: First screen photograph, where the backdrop is cut away (lower left of the suit at desktop, and the whole lower edge at phone); also the 'Graded for the site' texture sample
findings.fault: Cutting away the purple backdrop leaves hard, visible edges. A straight diagonal cut runs across the shoulder and lectern sign at the bottom left. At phone width, the head and collar end abruptly in slate and read as a floating head, not 'Mark at work'. This comes from the candidate's own keying, not from the stand-in photo, and the same treatment will apply to any new photo.
findings.who_objects: A senior official: a cut-out head with a crude edge looks home-made, which undermines the refined, serious standing an independent legal advisor needs. The founder asked for a photo of Mark speaking, graded into the house colours, not a cut-out.

findings.where: Nav ('Profile', 'Articles and talks', 'Blog'), and the lecture row's PDF link at the end of the article
findings.fault: All three nav items go to the same place, the article specimen (#article). 'Profile' lands on a blog post, not a profile. The lecture row is labelled PDF, but it also links to #article and offers no download.
findings.who_objects: The visitor: they click 'Profile' to check Mark's standing and get an article instead, then click 'PDF' and get nothing. Each dead end costs trust in a site whose one job is to get them to write.

findings.where: Whole page: the first screen and everything below it
findings.fault: Nothing shows Mark's standing. There are no named bodies or roles he has worked for, no regions or base country, and no qualification. His only claim, the lede's 'I advise multilateral development banks…', is unsupported, and the page jumps from that claim straight to the email.
findings.who_objects: A senior official choosing an individual against terms of reference: before writing they need to see that he has done PPP-law work for bodies like theirs, in their region (first-visit trust items 3 and 6, and 'feel the CV').

findings.where: First screen header, 'Mark M. Moseley' beside the logo
findings.fault: The logo beside the name is a home link, but the name is not a link. A visitor who clicks the name, the usual way home, gets no response.
findings.who_objects: A visitor on a deep page who tries to get back to the home page by clicking the name.

findings.where: Article specimen, the lecture row 'Streamlining the PPP Process…' under the article's last paragraph
findings.fault: A lecture with a different date and subject sits straight under the blog post's closing line, with no label such as 'Related' or 'Talks'. Its title starts a few pixels to the right of the column's left edge.
findings.who_objects: A reader who finishes the article and cannot tell whether the lecture belongs to it. Angélique will add rows like this one and needs a clear slot for them.

findings.where: Article specimen heading ('The World's Best…') and the type-pair text ('Mark's voice')
findings.fault: These use straight apostrophes, while the body text uses curly quotes ('one-size-fits-all', 'chapter topics'). The mismatch is most visible in the large display heading.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader of legal texts, who notices typographic slips at display size.
